papers.title: Planar PArcK is PSPACE-complete
papers.abstract: Partizan Arc Kayles, or PArcK, is a partizan combinatorial game on edge colored graphs, and is a generalization of the game Domineering. Previously, PArcK was shown to be PSPACE-complete on bipartite graphs. In this paper we show that PArcK is PSPACE-complete even when restricted to planar graphs of degree at most three by a reduction from Generalized Hex.

papers.title: Independent set reconfiguration is hard at treewidth four
papers.abstract: Independent Set Reconfiguration asks whether one of two given independent sets of equal size can be transformed into the other by moving one token at a time while keeping the occupied vertices independent. In token sliding, a token moves along an edge. In token jumping, it may move to any unoccupied vertex. For both rules, the problem is solvable in polynomial time on trees and is PSPACE-complete on graphs of treewidth at most $c$ for some fixed constant $c$. For each rule, the smallest treewidth bound that suffices for hardness has long been open. We narrow this gap by proving that both versions are NP-hard on graphs of treewidth four.

papers.title: Impatience Makes Matching NP-Hard
papers.abstract: Motivated by emerging applications such as online marketplaces and quantum switches, we study a dynamic bipartite matching model with impatient agents, where the two sides represent customers and suppliers. Agents of each type arrive according to an independent Poisson process, and the platform decides which pairs of agents to match. The agents are possibly impatient and may leave the system if not matched before their patience expires. The platform aims to maximize throughput, i.e., the number of matches per unit time. In this paper, we reveal an interesting phase transition in the computational hardness of throughput maximization. In particular, we show that approximating the optimal long-run throughput within a sufficiently small fixed relative error is NP-hard, even when all agents have rate-one exponential patience. This result implies a computational barrier to constructing near-optimal, efficiently executable matching policies that induce a matching process with fast mixing. On the other hand, when all agents on at least one side have infinite patience, we provide a simple polynomial-time algorithm that maximizes the throughput.

papers.title: Postselection on Halting and Reductions to the Halting Problem
papers.abstract: A probabilistic Turing machine is an ordinary Turing machine that may also toss fair coins, with no limit on its running time or memory. If it always halts, it decides only computable problems. Aaronson et al. studied machines that may run forever on some coin tosses, with the answer read only from the runs that halt. Suppose the correct answer must be more than twice as likely as the wrong one. They showed that these machines decide exactly the problems solvable with a fixed list of questions about the halting problem. They asked what happens when the correct answer need only be the more likely one. We show that the machines then decide exactly the problems solvable by asking such questions one after another, each chosen after the earlier answers. We also show that the factor two can be replaced by any fixed factor greater than one. A machine may promise two numbers: a lower bound on its probability of halting, and a lower bound on its probability of being right when it halts. From these two numbers we compute exactly how many questions fixed in advance the machine can replace. The main idea is that probability acts as a budget for how often a computable guess may change its mind. The results extend to oracle machines and to machines nested inside each other. Quantum machines decide the same problems.

papers.title: How Can Size, Ceiling, and Time Bounds Affect the Complexity of Nonuniform Automata Families?
papers.abstract: In the past literature, families of two-way finite automata and pushdown automata having limited resource-bounded complexity have been studied in direct connection to (mainstream) space-bounded complexity classes equipped with Karp-Lipton style advice of limited size when all inputs given to the automata have bounded length. We acknowledge three major factors--size, ceiling, and time--of such families, which have a significant impact on the computational/descriptional complexity of finite and pushdown automata families, where the "size" refers to the (stack-)state complexity, the "ceiling" refers to the maximum input length, and the "time" refers to the execution time of underlying automata. In this line of study, we further explore these effects caused by different sizes and ceilings. We exploit automata-based reducibility and translatability to space-bounded advised Turing machines and auxiliary automata.

papers.title: M\"obius-Pseudorandomness for Algebraic Circuits
papers.abstract: We define a notion of M\"obius-pseudorandomness for integer sequences generated by multivariate polynomials computed by small and simple algebraic circuits. This mirrors a related definition of Kalai that concerns boolean functions computed by small boolean circuits. We then prove M\"obius-pseudorandomness results for polynomials computed by algebraic circuits with few multiplication gates (of any depth), for polynomials with small-dimensional partial derivative space, and for the determinant and permanent. We conjecture that these results hold in general for polynomial-size algebraic circuits.

papers.title: Polynomial Swap Coboundary Expansion with Applications to LTCs and PCPs
papers.abstract: Swap coboundary expansion, introduced independently by Bafna--Minzer and Dikstein--Dinur, is a local-to-global property that underlies agreement tests in the low-acceptance regime and recent constructions of succinct PCPs. Previous works obtained bounds of $\exp(-O(\sqrt{r}))$ for the $r$-swap coboundary expansion of Chapman--Lubotzky complexes. We establish the first inverse-polynomial bounds for bounded-degree complexes: suitable skeleta of Kac--Moody--Steinberg (KMS) complexes have $r$-swap coboundary expansion at least $r^{-O(1)}$. Our theorem supplies a key ingredient in forthcoming work of Ben Yaacov--Dikstein--Liu, which obtains local tests for sparse algebraic codes with guarantees even at arbitrarily small acceptance probability. These tests use $\exp(\operatorname{poly}(1/\varepsilon))$ queries and guarantee that any word accepted with probability at least $\varepsilon$ agrees with a codeword on an $\varepsilon^{O(1)}$ fraction of coordinates. Separately, substituting our bound into the existing analysis of Bafna--Minzer--Vyas--Yun improves the soundness dependence of their two-query PCP construction, giving perfect completeness, soundness $\varepsilon$, and proof length $n(\log n)^{\exp(\operatorname{poly}(1/\varepsilon))}$. Our proof exploits the product structure of the groups arising in KMS complexes. The main new ingredient is a decomposition lemma for Dehn functions, which separates the analysis of group relations into independent problems on much smaller factors, with only polynomial overhead.

papers.title: Towards Understanding the Complexity of CAQE: A Proof-Theoretic Analysis of its Core Procedure
papers.abstract: CAQE (Clausal Abstraction for Quantifier Elimination) is currently the most successful algorithmic paradigm for solving Quantified Boolean Formulas (QBF) in practice, clearly dominating recent QBF competitions. While apparently being a very strong solver, not much is known about CAQE in theory. We propose a framework for formalising runs of the basic CAQE algorithm (where failed assumptions are not considered) as proofs in a proof system CAQE$^{\mathsf{Core}}$, which we use to analyse the algorithm proof-theoretically and which provides methods for future work to separate it from optimised versions of CAQE that are used in practice. We show that one can perform strategy extraction on the CAQE$^{\mathsf{Core}}$ proof system in such a way that strategy size serves as a lower bound for basic CAQE runs. Furthermore, we introduce a measure, which we call CAQE width, which not only acts as a lower bound on CAQE$^{\mathsf{Core}}$ proofs, but -- with the number of $\exists\forall$ alternations as exponent -- as an upper bound as well. Using this analysis, we prove that Q-resolution with an NP oracle simulates CAQE$^{\mathsf{Core}}$ on QCNFs of bounded quantifier alternation. The same holds for QCDCL (Quantified Conflict-Driven Clause Learning, formalised as a proof system) on $\Sigma_3^b$ QCNFs when purely propositional CDCL steps are not counted, after a simple preprocessing step. In this setting, both systems are indeed strictly stronger than CAQE$^{\mathsf{Core}}$, where the separation of QCDCL from CAQE$^{\mathsf{Core}}$ uses cube learning.

papers.title: Who Observes Whom: Network Rationalizability and Its Complexity
papers.abstract: Nash equilibrium and rationalizability sit at opposite informational extremes: the former presumes that each player knows all opponents' strategies, the latter that players reason from common knowledge of rationality alone. When visibility is partial and asymmetric, we study the solution concepts induced by a directed \emph{observation network} $G$ in which an edge $i\to j$ means that $i$ observes $j$'s strategy. A set of profiles is \emph{self-sustaining} if every profile in it can be justified, for every player, by conjectures from the same set that agree with everything the player observes. We consider \emph{point} conjectures (single profiles) and \emph{belief} conjectures (distributions over profiles). Both range from Nash equilibrium on the complete network to point- and correlated rationalizability on the empty network, and shrink monotonically as links are added. Network topology governs both behavior and complexity. A predicted profile can be found in polynomial time on the empty network, whereas a single link makes search $\mathsf{PPAD}$-hard: under one-sided two-player monitoring, the observed player's strategies are exactly her Nash equilibrium strategies. On hierarchical networks (transitive tournaments), membership reduces recursively to smaller games and admits polynomial-size certificates, placing verification in $\exists\mathbb{R}$, and in $\mathsf{P}$ for two players. On the directed three-cycle, however, iterated elimination may never terminate under either variant, and under point conjectures interior predictions may admit only infinite witness sets, a pathology that belief conjectures avoid in the same game. Finally, when only realized pure actions are observed, the solution set is guaranteed to be non-empty exactly when the network has no edges, and is computable in time $O(n|A|^2)$.

papers.title: Nearly Settling the Complexity of Connected $\varepsilon$-Envy-Free Cake Cutting
papers.abstract: Envy-free cake cutting has been one of the central problems in fair division. In cake cutting, agents' preferences over the cake are accessed through Robertson--Webb (RW) queries. For three or more agents, no algorithm that makes finitely many RW queries can always find a contiguous, exactly envy-free allocation. For contiguous $\varepsilon$-envy-free allocations, however, Hollender and Rubinstein~(JACM, 2025) showed that $\poly(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ RW queries suffice for four agents, leaving open whether such a bound is possible for five or more agents. In this paper, we establish a striking change in query complexity: $\poly(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ RW queries suffice for up to five agents, whereas $(1/\varepsilon)^{\Omega(1)}$ queries are necessary for seven or more agents, even when valuations are additive. Thus, we resolve the five-agent case and, more broadly, determine whether polylogarithmic query complexity is possible for every number of agents except six. We also explore the computational complexity of finding contiguous $\varepsilon$-envy-free allocations. When monotone Lipschitz valuations are given by polynomial-time evaluation procedures (e.g., arithmetic circuits and efficiently computable Turing machines), we show that an $\varepsilon$-envy-free division can be computed in polynomial time for five agents. In contrast, even for additive valuations, finding an $\varepsilon$-envy-free division is UEOPL-hard for every fixed number of agents $n\ge7$ and PPAD-complete for every fixed $n\ge13$.

papers.title: Separations Between Randomized and Exact Quantum Query Complexity for Boolean Functions
papers.abstract: We construct a family of total Boolean functions $F_{\mathrm{tot}}$ whose randomized and exact quantum query complexities satisfy $R(F_{\mathrm{tot}}) \ge Q_E(F_{\mathrm{tot}})^{2-o(1)}$. Chiruvella, Kayal, Mittal, Paraashar, and Saurabh (2026) also obtained a nearly quadratic separation for total functions in the query model by a different method. For every fixed $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$, we construct a family of partial Boolean functions $F_{\mathrm{par}}$ on $n$ bits satisfying $Q_E(F_{\mathrm{par}})=O_\varepsilon(1)$ and $R(F_{\mathrm{par}})=\Omega_\varepsilon(n^{1-\varepsilon})$. This matches the asymptotic separation previously obtained with bounded error (STOC 2021; SICOMP 2023). Lifting yields a family of partial communication functions $G_{\mathrm{par}}$ with $Q_E^{\mathrm{cc}}(G_{\mathrm{par}})=O_\varepsilon(\log n)$ and $R^{\mathrm{pub,cc}}(G_{\mathrm{par}})=\Omega_\varepsilon(n^{1-\varepsilon})$, where $n$ is the total number of input bits held by the two parties.

papers.title: Approximate Computation via Le Cam Simulability
papers.abstract: We propose a decision-theoretic framework for computational complexity, complementary to classical theory: moving from syntactic exactness (Turing / Shannon) to semantic simulability (Le Cam). While classical theory classifies problems by the cost of exact solution, modern computation often seeks only decision-valid approximations. We introduce a framework where "computation" is viewed as the efficient simulation of a target statistical experiment within a bounded risk distortion (Le Cam deficiency). We formally define computational deficiency ($\delta_{\text{poly}}$) and use it to construct the complexity class LeCam-P (Decision-Robust Polynomial Time), characterizing problems that may be syntactically hard but semantically easy to approximate. We show that classical Karp reductions can be viewed as zero-deficiency simulations, and that approximate reductions correspond to bounded deficiency. Furthermore, we establish the No-Free-Transfer Inequality, showing that strictly invariant representations inevitably destroy decision-relevant information. This framework offers a statistical perspective on approximation theory, bridging the gap between algorithmic complexity and decision theory.

papers.title: Exact Algorithms for Edge Deletion to Cactus
papers.abstract: We study two related problems on simple, un-directed graphs: Edge Deletion to Cactus and Spanning Tree to Cactus. Edge Deletion to Cactus has been known to be NP-hard on general graphs at least since 1988. We show improved exact algorithms for the former and a polynomial time algorithm for the latter.

papers.title: Affine Combiners for Reed-Solomon Proximity Gaps
papers.abstract: Reed-Solomon proximity gaps establish soundness guarantees for protocols that test received words through random combinations. For length-$n$ codes over $\mathbb{F}_q$, classical scalar combiners achieve error $O(n/q)$ in the unique-decoding regime, with larger known bounds near the Johnson radius. We prove smaller error bounds using affine combiners, which combine two received words $f,g$ as $f(x)+(\alpha+\beta x)g(x)$, where $\alpha,\beta$ are independent uniform elements of $\mathbb{F}_q$. For output degree bound $d=\rho n$, fixed $\rho\in(0,1)$ and $0<\eta<1-\sqrt{\rho}$, and sufficiently large block length $n$, we prove mutual correlated agreement (MCA) with one coordinate of agreement loss at threshold $A=\lceil(\sqrt{\rho}+\eta)n\rceil$, with error $O_{\rho,\eta}\left(\frac{1}{q}+\frac{n^2}{q^2}\right)$. The result holds over arbitrary evaluation domains in every finite field, including prime and binary extension fields. The agreement threshold can approach the Johnson threshold, beyond unique decoding. For $q\ge n^2$, our error is $O_{\rho,\eta}(1/q)$, an asymptotic factor-$n$ separation from scalar combiners: we prove that their worst-case MCA error is $\Omega_{\rho,\eta}(n/q)$ at the same agreement threshold and with the same one-coordinate loss. We also prove that affine combiners incur worst-case error $\Omega_{\rho,\eta}(n/q)$ when no agreement loss is allowed. Thus one coordinate of agreement loss is necessary for our guarantee; this relaxation of standard MCA reduces the guaranteed common agreement fraction by at most $1/n$. We also extend the result to $k$-variate Reed-Muller codes on subfield grids, obtaining MCA error $O_{\rho,\eta,k}(q^{-k})$ for fixed $\rho,\eta,k$, sufficiently large $n$, and $q\ge n^{k+1}$, with agreement loss $n^{1-1/k}$.

papers.title: Primal/Dual Method for the Grothendieck Constant
papers.abstract: We determine the hundredths digit of the real Grothendieck constant by proving $1.773 \leq K_G \leq 1.7799$. Furthermore, numerical heuristics suggest the estimate $K_G \approx 1.779$. We start by simplifying the Gaussian duality theory of $K_G$, based on Hermite projection games and Krivine rounding schemes. The bounds are obtained by a heuristic primal/dual search for these objects, followed by rigorous {\em certification} of their values. The search and certification are performed using AI tools, and in particular the rigorous certificates are very large (analytical reductions to thousands of numerical inequalities).

papers.title: A New Characterization of Streaming Decidability of Boolean CSPs Under Deletions
papers.abstract: We characterize the single-pass streaming space complexity of Boolean CSP satisfiability in the strict-turnstile model for every fixed constraint language $\Gamma$ of $k$-ary Boolean relations that is not trivially satisfiable. Constraints can be inserted or deleted with nonnegative multiplicities; satisfiability is decided for those remaining at the end. While Sharma and Velusamy [ESA 2026] characterized insertion-only complexity via non-redundancy (up to logarithmic factors), we show that strict-turnstile complexity is governed by the integer capturing degree. For $R\subseteq\{0,1\}^k$, let $d_R$ be the minimum degree of an integer-coefficient polynomial vanishing exactly on $R$ over the Boolean hypercube, and set $d_\Gamma=\max_{R\in\Gamma}d_R$. On polynomial-length streams, we obtain an $O_k(n^{d_\Gamma}\operatorname{polylog} n)$-space randomized algorithm and an $\Omega_k(n^{d_\Gamma}/\log n)$ lower bound for all algorithms. Moreover, our algorithm outputs a sparse instance preserving every satisfying assignment. This yields, to our knowledge, the first insertion-only versus turnstile separation for streaming CSPs. It also differs from the Fourier-degree characterization of exact optimization by Kol, Paramonov, Saxena, and Yu [ITCS 2023]. For $k\ge3$, $k$-XOR with literals has three distinct space complexities: $\widetilde\Theta(n)$ for insertion-only satisfiability, $\widetilde\Theta(n^{\lceil k/2\rceil})$ for strict-turnstile satisfiability, and $\widetilde\Theta(n^k)$ for exact optimization in either model.

papers.title: Metric Dimension Parameterized by Bag-Connected Treewidth and Bag-Connected Pathwidth
papers.abstract: The metric dimension of a graph is the minimum size of a set of vertices whose distance vectors distinguish all vertices of the graph. We prove that \MetricDimension{} is NP-complete on planar graphs of treewidth and bag-connected treewidth exactly three. The graphs in our construction have no induced cycle longer than four and have (prefix-connected) pathwidth at most four. In particular, the problem admits no XP algorithm parameterized by bag-connected treewidth unless $\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}$. This answers questions of Bonnet and Purohit and of Bousquet, Deschamps, and Parreau. We prove that the problem is fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by bag-connected pathwidth.

papers.title: The multiplicative complexity of the three-bit low-half multiplier
papers.abstract: We prove that the multiplicative complexity of the three-bit low-half multiplier is six, giving a structural, enumeration-free lower-bound proof valid against unrestricted nonlinear reuse in Boolean XOR-AND circuits. The value was first established by SAT searches of the first author and independently confirmed by the second author. An explicit six-AND circuit supplies the upper bound. The lower bound combines derivatives, quadratic products, complementary minors, and extraction modulo a Boolean ideal. Independent finite checks accompany the arguments. $\mathrm{MC}(M_3)=6$ is fully formalized in Lean 4, using only Lean's three standard axioms (propositional extensionality, choice and quotient soundness).

papers.title: Simulating Space Bounded Read-$k$ PTMs with Space Bounded Read-Once PTMs
papers.abstract: We show that read-$k$ Probabilistic Turing Machines with bounded space $S$ and running time $T$ can be simulated by read-once Probabilistic Turing Machines with error $\varepsilon$, running in space $ O(k^2 (S + \log (n+ T)) + \log (1/\epsilon))$ and time $\frac{1}{\varepsilon} \cdot 2^{O\left(k^2\left(S+\log(n+T) \right)\right)}$. As a direct consequence we show that read-$k$ $\mathsf{BPL}$ is equal to $\mathsf{BPL}$, for any constant $k$. Recently OpenAI announced that $\mathsf{BPL} = \mathsf{L}$. If this is true then our result immediately implies that read-$k$ $\mathsf{BPL}$ is equal to $\mathsf{L}$.
